subChunks.title: Interfaces

storyBeats.text: Eldrin taps two completely different creatures — a Wizard and a Stone Golem — and says they both signed the same Healable contract.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: An interface is a contract. I do not care what you are — Wizard, Dragon, Golem — as long as you promise to implement these methods. Unlike a class, you can sign as many contracts as you wish.

storyBeats.label: Multiple interfaces

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: A class may implement many interfaces — that is Java's answer to the limitation of single inheritance. Interfaces are contracts; a class can hold many contracts simultaneously.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Define an interface Describable with one method: String describe(). Implement it in two classes: Weapon (returns "Sword: 40 dmg") and Armour (returns "Shield: 30 def"). Store both in a Describable[] array and print each description.
guidedPractice.hint: Use a for-each loop over the Describable array and call d.describe() on each element.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: What is a Java interface? How does it differ from an abstract class, and why would you prefer an interface?

questions.prompt: How many interfaces can a Java class implement?
options: Only as many as it has methods
questions.explanation: A class can implement any number of interfaces, separated by commas: class Foo implements A, B, C { ... }.

questions.prompt: You can create an instance of a Java interface directly using new.
questions.explanation: Interfaces cannot be instantiated. You create instances of classes that implement the interface. (Anonymous classes and lambda expressions can provide inline implementations.)

subChunks.title: Polymorphism

storyBeats.text: Eldrin lines up a Wizard, a Dragon, and a Golem — all very different — and issues a single command.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Polymorphism is the power to give one command and have every creature respond in its own unique way. I say speak(); the Dragon roars, the Golem rumbles, the Wizard recites verse. One command — many forms.

storyBeats.label: One command, many responses

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: This is the magic of coding against an abstraction. Tomorrow you add a Golem — you need not change a single line of the loop. The new type simply fulfils the same contract.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Create an interface Attacker with method void attack(). Implement it in Swordsman (prints "Swings sword!"), Archer (prints "Shoots arrow!"), and Mage (prints "Casts spell!"). Store all three in a List<Attacker> and call attack() on each.
guidedPractice.hint: Declare the list as List<Attacker> party = new ArrayList<>() and add each instance to it.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain polymorphism in Java. Why is it powerful to write code against an interface rather than a concrete class?

questions.prompt: What determines which version of an overridden method runs when called through a parent-type reference?
options: The actual type of the object at runtime
The declared type of the reference variable
The first class in the inheritance chain
questions.answer: The actual type of the object at runtime
questions.explanation: This is dynamic dispatch — Java determines at runtime which method to call based on the object's actual type, not the declared type of the reference.
The reference type is Base, but the actual object is a Child. At runtime, Java calls Child's overridden print().

subChunks.title: Default Methods & Composition vs Inheritance

storyBeats.text: Eldrin demonstrates an Eagle that flies — and lands for free without any extra work, courtesy of the Flyable contract's default method.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Default methods let you evolve an interface without breaking every class that implements it. Add a new default method and existing implementors get it automatically — they can override if they want, or accept the default.

storyBeats.label: Default method

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: And composition — the wisest design pattern of all. A DragonRider is not a Dragon and not a Rider; it has a Dragon and has a Rider. Components can be swapped, tested, and reused independently.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Define interface Printable with abstract String content() and a default void print() that prints "[content()]" (with square brackets). Implement it in Report and Invoice classes with different content. Call print() on both.
guidedPractice.hint: The default print() method should call this.content() and wrap it in square brackets.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: What are default methods in Java interfaces, and why were they introduced? When would you prefer composition over inheritance?

questions.prompt: Which keyword is used to define a method with a body inside a Java interface?
questions.explanation: The default keyword (introduced in Java 8) allows interface methods to have a default implementation that implementing classes can use or override.
Bot inherits the greet() default method. When called, it invokes name() which Bot implements as "R2D2".

questions.prompt: You are building a game with a Character class. You need characters to be able to fly, swim, and cast spells — but not all characters do all three. What design approach is most flexible?
options: Define Flyable, Swimmable, and Castable as interfaces; each character class implements the relevant ones
Create a single abstract Character class with all three methods abstract
Use one deep inheritance hierarchy: SwimmingFlyingCastingCharacter extends FlyingCastingCharacter
Add boolean flags (canFly, canSwim, canCast) to the base class
questions.answer: Define Flyable, Swimmable, and Castable as interfaces; each character class implements the relevant ones
questions.explanation: Interfaces model capabilities cleanly — a character implements only the interfaces matching its abilities. Using inheritance for this would require complex hierarchies or code duplication.
